source.title: Scaling Laws for Data Filtering -- Data Curation cannot be Compute Agnostic
source.authors: Sachin Goyal; Pratyush Maini; Zachary Chase Lipton; Aditi Raghunathan; J. Kolter

record.file_problem: The full paper, including appendices, is present; no relevant cutoff or garbling noted.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own CLIP experiments and refines scaling-law formulations for heterogeneous data and repeated training. It argues that a single homogeneous-data law does not capture these effects.
record.gate_note: The paper studies contrastive image-text models and downstream zero-shot error or accuracy, not held-out language-model pretraining loss or parameter/token scaling. Its cited results from prior work are not recorded as rows. The study's measured outcomes are downstream performance, data-utility scaling parameters, and validation of estimated curves.
record.test_reason: The study fits power-law-form scaling laws of the form y = a·n^b + d to CLIP zero-shot error under repeated and heterogeneous data. It argues that a single homogeneous law cannot capture these effects and adds pool-specific exponents and repetition decay. It then checks the modified law's estimates against held-out pool combinations and against pretrained models from Cherti et al. This bears on V5, V6 and V7. There are no language-model loss, allocation or architecture sweeps.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that data curation cannot be compute-agnostic: limited high-quality data loses utility with repetition. Their scaling laws, with pool-specific utility and repetition half-lives, estimate the performance of pool mixtures without training on them. The authors add that existing laws treat data as homogeneous and that this is inadequate.
record.recipe_differences: Uses CLIP contrastive training, heterogeneous image-text data pools, repeated-data utility parameters, and downstream zero-shot error/accuracy rather than language-model held-out pretraining loss over parameters, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Filtering aggressiveness and the best pool combination change with compute. Fitted utility and repetition parameters vary across data pools; fitting with a single shared repetition half-life gives higher L2 fitting loss than pool-specific half-lives. The experiments use a fixed batch size of 4096.

fits_no_version.finding: The best data-filtering threshold shifts with compute. Aggressive filtering is best at low compute and less aggressive filtering at high compute. Unfiltered data beats LAION-filtered data beyond 450M samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal data-curation aggressiveness depends on the ratio of training compute to the size of the high-quality pool.

record.problems: The experiments use a fixed batch size of 4096, and the authors state that their laws do not account for batch-size variation. They also note uncertainty about whether scaling parameters remain consistent when pool size changes by orders of magnitude and about how pool mixing changes data diversity. Several plotted outcomes have no numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional outcome rows omitted. Cited findings from prior work were excluded.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no sweep over parameters, tokens or compute; the model size is fixed (ViT-B/32 at medium scale).

There is no test of small-run fits predicting runs orders of magnitude larger. The combination extrapolation stays within about 5x compute, and the Cherti models may not be a true out-of-range extrapolation.
No comparison of model shape at a fixed parameter count.
Untested: other modalities beyond image-text contrastive training, fine-tuning, transfer, and validation loss as opposed to downstream error.
Untested: language-model downstream tasks, and predicting downstream performance from pretraining loss.

missing.what: Fitted b and τ for CLIP-score pools. The b values are Top10% -0.14, 10–20% -0.15, 20–30% -0.14, 30–40% -0.12, 40–50% -0.11, which is not strictly monotonic. Bears on how exponents depend on the data.
Fitted b and τ for T-MARS pools on the 18-task average (b -0.18, -0.15, -0.12, -0.08). The exponents differ from the ImageNet fits for the same pools.
Fitting-method sensitivity. SciPy and gradient-based fits were unstable and initialization-sensitive, extrapolating badly to mixtures, so the authors used grid search.
The effective-data formulation (Muennighoff-style) cannot model mixtures of pools. Constraining all pools to one decay factor gave a significantly higher loss on the fit points themselves.
A sweep of the τ-merging exponent k. The minimum fitting loss is at k=1, matching the derived N̂/N rule for contrastive pairs.

record.verdict_notes: This is not one of the original sources. The measure is downstream zero-shot error, not pretraining loss, and the model size is fixed, so only samples seen is scaled. The record's V6 links on the filtering-comparison rows (R1–R6) were wrong: those rows rank curation strategies rather than test scaling predictability. No prediction-error numbers are reported anywhere, so V6 support rests on plots and the authors' wording. The authors themselves flag the fixed batch size (4096) and the unknown stability of the parameters at 100x pool size.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss or sweep over language-model parameters, tokens, and compute.
The paper estimates CLIP downstream error for data mixtures and pretrained CLIP models; it does not test whether small language-model runs predict the pretraining loss of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep over language-model parameter count and token count.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

Tests image-text CLIP training with repeated data and heterogeneous data pools, using downstream zero-shot error rather than held-out pretraining loss. Does not test other modalities, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes beyond the stated CLIP evaluations.
Tests zero-shot performance on visual classification and retrieval tasks for CLIP, not language-model downstream tasks or general downstream performance across model families.

Tests variation in fitted data-utility parameters across pools and a fitting choice for repetition half-life. Does not test language-model parameter-counting choices, training schedules, or compute-optimal parameter/token splits.

rows.subject: CLIP models trained on the DataComp medium-scale pool
rows.operation_detail: Compared training on LAION-filtered data with training on the unfiltered common crawl pool.
rows.value: LAION filtering achieves an increase of 7.5% zero-shot accuracy
rows.note: The paper reports the difference at 128M training iterations; it does not give the absolute accuracies in the text.
rows.check: This compares two filtering methods at one compute level (+7.5% for LAION-filtered at 128M). It does not measure whether downstream performance scales predictably, so it is not a V6 row. It records a fact about data curation.

rows.subject: CLIP models trained on the DataComp medium-scale pool
rows.operation_detail: Compared training on the unfiltered common crawl pool with training on LAION-filtered data.
rows.value: Unfiltered common crawl outperforms LAION-filtered data beyond 450M iterations
rows.note: The paper attributes the reversal to repeated exposure to the smaller filtered pool.
rows.check: 'Reversed' against V6 is wrong. The accuracy of LAION-filtered training plateaus with repetition, and no-filtering overtakes it beyond 450M samples. This shows the curve bending away from a single power law under repetition (V7). It does not show downstream performance failing to improve with scale.

source_check.correct: The listed b values are correct. State: observed for V7; partial for V5 because Equation 3 includes epoch-dependent utility decay rather than a single fixed-exponent power law.
source_check.problem: The observed state does not distinguish support for setup-dependent parameters from qualification of V5's unchanged power-law form.

rows.note: The text interprets smaller half-life as lower data diversity.
rows.check: The fitted half-life τ varies across pools (4.36, 4.27, 3.00, 1.55 in the Figure 4 legend). This is a fit-dependence result. The row lacks these numbers, and they should be added.

rows.subject: Pretrained CLIP models from Cherti et al. (2023)
rows.size_stated: Models across 2 architectures, pool sizes 80M, 400M, and 2B, and compute budgets ranging from 3B to 34B samples
rows.operation_detail: Applied the proposed scaling law to estimate ImageNet zero-shot error for previously trained models.
rows.baseline: Actual model errors shown as comparison points
rows.value: The paper states that the proposed laws predict error with high accuracy
rows.note: The paper reports an aggregate statement across the described architectures, pool sizes, and compute budgets; per-model values are plotted.
rows.check: The text says only that the law predicts error 'with a high accuracy' and reports no error values. It is unclear whether the parameters were fitted on these Cherti models or extrapolated from smaller runs, so this row does not establish extrapolation.

source_check.correct: State: observed for V6 according to the authors' qualitative assessment; partial for V5 because the predictions incorporate diminishing utility under repetition.
source_check.problem: The observed state for V5 overlooks the repetition correction required by the fitted law.

rows.subject: CLIP models fit with shared versus pool-specific repetition parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared scaling-curve fitting with a common repetition half-life τ for all pools against separate τ values per pool.

rows.baseline: Shared τ across pools gives a worse (higher) L2 fitting error
rows.value: Using different τ values for each pool gives a lower fitting error
rows.note: The text explicitly reports the direction of the fitting-loss difference; numerical values are plotted.
rows.check: The baseline field holds a result rather than a baseline. The baseline is the shared-τ fit and the value is the lower L2 error with per-pool τ.

relationships.condition: CLIP ViT-B/32 contrastive training on DataComp-medium quality pools, ImageNet and 18-task zero-shot error
relationships.reason: A power-law form with an irreducible term fits each quality pool, and the estimated curves for combinations agree with held-out test points and with the Cherti ViT-B models (R8, R10, R11).
relationships.display_finding: Power laws with irreducible terms fitted each quality pool, and predicted combinations agreed with held-out test points and the Cherti ViT-B models.

relationships.condition: Repeated-data (multi-epoch) CLIP training on heterogeneous pools
relationships.reason: The plain power law does not suffice under repetition. The exponent must decay per epoch with pool-specific half-lives, and a shared τ fits much worse (R8, R12).
relationships.display_finding: The exponent needed to decay each epoch with pool-specific half-lives, while a shared decay parameter fit substantially worse.
